questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality Involving Exponential Functions with the Same Exponents and a Polynomial
questions.worked_solution:
First, we move all the terms to the left side of the inequality and factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{e}^{2x-1}<-8{e}^{2x-1}-6x{e}^{2x-1} \\ {x}^{2}{e}^{2x-1}+6x{e}^{2x-1}+8{e}^{2x-1} & <0 \\ ({x}^{2}+6x+8){e}^{2x-1} & <0 \\ (x+4)(x+2){e}^{2x-1} & <0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we divide both sides by ${e}^{2x-1}$ and get

$$
(x+4)(x+2)<0.
$$

This represents an upwards parabola whose roots are at $x=-4$ and $x=-2.$ The parabola is below the $x$-axis when $-4<x<-2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14042952/assets/15a31e60a938b604b96ade5e6868c658a2e2f0a53fe2a5f53a032093155e8aee.png)

Therefore, the solution is $-4<x<-2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality Involving Exponential Functions with Different Exponents and a Polynomial
questions.worked_solution:
First, we move all the terms to the left side of the inequality and factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{3}^{6x+1}x & <-{3}^{6x}{x}^{2} \\ {3}^{6x}{x}^{2}-{3}^{6x+1}x & <0 \\ {3}^{6x}({x}^{2}-3x) & <0 \\ {3}^{6x}x(x-3) & <0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we divide both sides by ${3}^{6x}$ and get

$$
x(x-3)<0.
$$

This represents an upwards parabola whose roots are at $x=0$ and $x=3.$ The parabola is below the $x$-axis when $0<x<3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14042952/assets/8582e3a512cc29618a3e2db9dda4478481167eefcf0a2fbdfb7d33e5786ba62e.png)

Therefore, the solution is  $0<x<3.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we move all the terms to the left side of the inequality and factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\cdot {5}^{7x} & \ge {5}^{7x-3} \\ {x}^{3}\cdot {5}^{7x}-{5}^{7x-3} & \ge 0 \\ ({x}^{3}-{5}^{-3})\cdot {5}^{7x} & \ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we divide both sides by ${5}^{7x}$ and get

$$
{x}^{3}-{5}^{-3}\ge 0.
$$

Finally, we can solve this inequality using familiar methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3} & \ge {5}^{-3} \\ \sqrt[3]{{x}^{3}} & \ge \sqrt[3]{{5}^{-3}} \\ x & \ge {({5}^{-3})}^{1/3} \\ x & \ge {5}^{-1} \\ x & \ge \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the inequality is $x\ge \frac{1}{5}.$

First, we move all the terms to the left side of the inequality and factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x\cdot {5}^{x+6}-{5}^{x+6} & <8\cdot {5}^{x+6} \\ 3x\cdot {5}^{x+6}-{5}^{x+6}-8\cdot {5}^{x+6} & <0 \\ (3x-1-8){5}^{x+6} & <0 \\ (3x-9){5}^{x+6} & <0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we divide both sides by ${5}^{x+6}$ and solve the resulting inequality using familiar techniques:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-9 & <0 \\ 3x & <9 \\ x & <3\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to the inequality above is $x<3.$

First, we move all the terms to the left side of the inequality and factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{4-5x}x & <{3}^{2-5x}{x}^{2} \\ {3}^{4-5x}x-{3}^{2-5x}{x}^{2} & <0 \\ ({3}^{2}x-{x}^{2})\cdot {3}^{2-5x} & <0 \\ (9x-{x}^{2})\cdot {3}^{2-5x} & <0 \\ x(9-x)\cdot {3}^{2-5x} & <0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we divide both sides by ${3}^{2-5x}$ and get

$$
x(9-x)<0.
$$

This represents a downwards parabola whose roots are at $x=0$ and $x=9.$ The parabola is below the $x$-axis when  $x<0$ or $x>9.$
